cards.headline:
Does a design system steer
what a coding agent writes
cards.body: In 30 runs, agents given the design system as an npm package hand-wrote no components; a prose styleguide fell short.

blocks.x: The author built a design system before agents started writing UI: three-tier tokens, 14 Angular components, type declarations and an llms.client.txt shipped inside the npm package, plus a token resolver over MCP. Then he asked whether any of it changes what a coding agent produces.

The test: one Angular dashboard, a byte-identical prompt, fresh sessions, and five arms — specification and Figma frames only (A), plus a prose styleguide (A′), plus the npm packages (B), plus llms.client.txt (C), plus the MCP resolver (D). Thirty scored runs, with scorers and falsifiers committed in advance.

Shipping the system is a step function; writing it down is not. Without the package, the agent hand-writes 12 or 13 of 13 components and the app acquires around 90 custom properties; with it, zero and zero.

Accessibility mattered more than consistency: agents got colours right from Figma but shipped serious contrast failures. Agents never hallucinated the component API in 30 runs. Using the library cost more per generation, and the MCP resolver added no measurable improvement over the text file.
“The design system does not make the agent smarter or more correct. It decides who ends up owning the code it writes.” The author calls it a case study, not a benchmark.
